items.title: Charles L. Dufour Interview, 1958-05-14
items.q: And I've always, under certain conditions, loved Papa Celesta, for example.

ctx.x: me. He said, they do more far off. Didn't you look a little bit like before? More than I did. Well, you said that the gaze didn't offend you. You know, did a lot of people say that they were just rotten, gutter-clapted, claps? A lot of people did. And I wouldn't doubt for a moment that I went through a period in which I felt that. But I mean, the overall feeling that I have now is that it didn't offend me, and that doesn't defend me, although I would never go out and seek it. Keep quiet. And I would go out and…

And I've always, under certain conditions, loved Papa Celesta, for example. And when the Saints go marching in, or hear Susha and his group play, particularly Edmonds singing that grapple-throated, if ever I ceased to love, version of the Moneygrass. But that's the best answer

I can give you. I just feel confident that if my memory is correct, there were times where I, when I did, looked down my nose in jazz. And you said a great number of people that did. I think that there were... I think there were many that did. Would you say a majority of New Orleans? No, I'd say the majority accepted it. I'd say the majority accepted it and recognized it as... Well, you see, here's the point. If a person was a dancer and a dancegoer and a party man, and he'd hear it at the party and hear it to…
